subject: maths
stem: A batsman scores 42, 35, 60, 28 and 50 runs in five innings. What is his average score per innings?
rationale: The five scores total 215, and 215 ÷ 5 = 43. Two steps, both routine, which is what places it at the floor of the tier. Numeric format is deliberate: the characteristic error is dividing by 4 after miscounting the innings, and an option list containing 53.75 would make that error visible enough to self-correct.

subject: maths
stem: Which of these fractions is the largest?
rationale: Over a common denominator of 120 these are 72, 75, 80 and 70, so 2/3 is largest. Every value sits between 0.58 and 0.67, which is the point: they are close enough that eyeballing fails and the candidate must actually convert. B (5/8) is the near miss at 0.625 and will take most of the wrong responses; D (7/12) is the smallest and attracts anyone comparing numerators alone.

subject: maths
stem: A shopkeeper buys a chair for ₹1,200 and sells it for ₹1,500. What is the profit percentage?
rationale: Profit is ₹300 on a cost of ₹1,200, so 300/1200 = 25%. B (20%) is the single most common error in profit-and-loss: it computes 300/1500, taking the profit as a fraction of the selling price rather than the cost. The item exists to catch exactly that, so B is placed adjacent to the key where an unsure candidate will hover.

subject: maths
stem: Two bells ring at intervals of 12 minutes and 18 minutes. They ring together at 9:00 am. After how many minutes will they next ring together?
rationale: 12 = 2² x 3 and 18 = 2 x 3², so the LCM is 2² x 3² = 36 minutes. The seductive wrong answer is the HCF, 6, and the second is 216 from multiplying the two intervals. Numeric format means both score 0 rather than being cued by an option list — deciding whether a situation calls for LCM or HCF is the whole skill here.

subject: maths
stem: A rectangular field is 24 m long and 16 m wide. How much fencing is needed to enclose it completely?
rationale: Fencing follows the perimeter: 2 x (24 + 16) = 80 m. D (384 m) is the area, 24 x 16, and is the dominant error — the word 'enclose' is the only signal distinguishing the two, so the item measures reading as much as arithmetic. A (40 m) adds the sides once instead of twice. C (160 m) doubles the perimeter.

subject: maths
stem: What is the simple interest on ₹5,000 at 8% per annum for 3 years, in rupees?
rationale: 5,000 x 8 x 3 / 100 = 1,200. A single formula applied once, with no conversion or reversal, which is what makes it easy. The common error is returning 6,200 — the amount rather than the interest — and the stem says 'simple interest' explicitly so that the error is the candidate's, not the item's.

subject: maths
stem: Which number does not belong with the others?
rationale: 8, 27 and 125 are 2³, 3³ and 5³; 45 is not a perfect cube. The set is chosen so that exactly one rule fits — 45 is not a perfect square either, so there is no second reading that reaches a different answer. Ambiguity is the usual failure of odd-one-out items and this one is built to avoid it.

subject: maths
stem: A container holds 2.5 litres of water. How many millilitres is this?
rationale: One litre is 1,000 millilitres, so 2.5 litres is 2,500 ml. Every distractor is a power-of-ten slip in one direction or the other, which is precisely how this error occurs in practice — candidates rarely get the conversion conceptually wrong, they misplace the decimal. A floor item: a candidate who misses it is not ready for the rest of the paper.

subject: maths
stem: If CAT is written as 3-1-20, how is DOG written in the same code?
rationale: Each letter maps to its alphabet position: A = 4, O = 15, G = 7. B (4-14-7) miscounts O as 14, the off-by-one that comes from counting the alphabet from a nearby anchor rather than carefully. C shifts every letter back one, A shifts every letter forward one — both are candidates who find a pattern in the example and apply it to the wrong thing.

subject: maths
stem: A father is three times as old as his son. In 10 years, he will be twice as old as his son. How old is the son now?
rationale: If the son is s then the father is 3s, and 3s + 10 = 2(s + 10) gives s = 10 — a son of 10 and a father of 30, who in ten years are 20 and 40. Moderate because it needs two relationships from two points in time held simultaneously; a candidate who works only from the present cannot start. Every distractor is a plausible age, so none can be eliminated on sense alone.

subject: maths
stem: A bag contains 4 red balls and 6 blue balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is red?
rationale: There are 10 balls of which 4 are red, so 4/10 = 2/5. B (2/3) is the reason this sits at moderate rather than easy: it is 4/6, the ratio of red to blue, used where the denominator must be the total. C (3/5) is the probability of blue — the right method answering the wrong question. A assumes one favourable outcome in four.

subject: maths
stem: Find the next number in the series: 5, 11, 23, 47, 95, ___
rationale: Each term is double the previous plus one: 95 x 2 + 1 = 191. The differences 6, 12, 24, 48 double as well, so reading the series either way converges on 191 — a property worth having, because it means a candidate who finds a valid route is not punished for finding the other one. C (190) doubles and forgets the +1. B (189) doubles and subtracts. A (143) repeats the difference of 48 instead of doubling it.

subject: maths
stem: A pipe fills a tank in 4 hours. A leak at the bottom would empty the full tank in 6 hours. With the leak present, how many hours does the pipe take to fill the tank?
rationale: The rates oppose: 1/4 − 1/6 = 1/12 of the tank per hour, so 12 hours. Difficult because the candidate must recognise that one rate is negative before any arithmetic starts — adding them gives 5/12 and an answer of 2.4 hours, which is faster than the pipe alone and should fail a sanity check that many candidates will not apply. Numeric format denies them the chance to notice that 2.4 looks wrong next to 12.

subject: maths
stem: The price of a book is increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. Compared with the original price, the final price is:
rationale: 1.20 x 0.80 = 0.96, so the price ends 4% below where it started. B (the same) is the intuitive answer and should take most of the wrong responses — the two percentages look symmetrical but apply to different bases, the second to the already-inflated price. C offers the same error with the sign flipped. D (40% less) adds the percentages. Difficult despite trivial arithmetic: the whole item is whether the candidate notices the base has moved.

subject: maths
stem: A trader gives a 20% discount on the marked price and still makes a 20% profit on an item that cost him ₹2,000. What was the marked price, in rupees?
rationale: A 20% profit on ₹2,000 means a selling price of ₹2,400, and that is 80% of the marked price, so the marked price is 2,400 ÷ 0.8 = ₹3,000. Difficult because it chains two percentages on different bases and runs the second one backwards — dividing where the instinct is to multiply. The characteristic error is 2,400 x 1.2 = 2,880, applying the discount forwards; the trap is that 2,880 is close enough to 3,000 to look plausible.
